paragraphs: ACES investigates whether a generative model can invent programming problems that are both varied and challenging. Its setting is Python puzzles, where the aim is to produce difficult but solvable tasks. The approach jointly pursues difficulty and diversity, so generating more problems is tied to exploring different combinations of programming skills.

The method describes each puzzle using semantic descriptors generated by a language model, such as string manipulation or dynamic programming. These descriptors organize the space of possible problems. Difficulty is measured empirically from Llama-3-70B's success rate: lower success means higher difficulty. ACES repeatedly asks a language model to target different descriptors, using previously generated puzzles as examples to guide further exploration.

The resulting problems were more diverse and challenging than those from the tested baseline methods. Across 11 code language models, the authors report that they were three times more challenging than existing Python benchmark problems on average. This finding concerns difficulty measured through model performance, connecting problem generation to the observed capabilities of the solvers.
neurips-2024-aces-generating-a-diversity.tldr: ACES generates varied Python puzzles by targeting programming skills and using solver success rates to guide difficulty.

paragraphs: Architect generates complex, interactive 3D environments by drawing on the scene composition abilities of pretrained 2D image models. It uses diffusion-based inpainting to add objects to images, visual perception models to isolate those objects, and depth estimation to translate the generated content into 3D space. This connects image generation with environment construction for robotics and embodied AI.

A central obstacle is that generated images do not inherently supply reliable camera parameters or depth scale. Architect starts from a simulated background whose camera and depth are known. It renders that background and then inpaints foreground content, allowing the existing geometric cues to guide generation. This helps control the geometry needed to project image content into 3D point clouds.

The process proceeds hierarchically and iteratively, adding large furniture and smaller objects to enrich a scene. It can start from text, floor plans, or an existing arrangement, supporting both creation and refinement. Experiments report more realistic and complex environments than existing methods, supporting the usefulness of controlled image generation for constructing embodied environments.
neurips-2024-architect-generating-vivid-.tldr: Architect uses geometrically guided, hierarchical image inpainting to build realistic and complex interactive 3D environments.

paragraphs: Continuous attractors describe recurrent systems that can retain a continuously valued quantity indefinitely. Their difficulty is structural fragility: even tiny changes to the governing dynamics can destroy the exact attractor. This seems especially problematic for biological memory, where the underlying system is continually perturbed. The paper asks whether losing the exact mathematical structure also destroys its practical memory function.

The authors observe that perturbed systems can have very different eventual behavior while behaving similarly over finite periods. Using persistent manifold theory and fast-slow analysis, they identify a surviving slow manifold, a structure along which the system changes gradually. They relate motion within this structure to the perturbation size and use that relationship to bound the resulting memory error.

Experiments train recurrent neural networks on analog memory tasks and support the emergence and generalization of these approximate memory systems. The distinction between indefinite storage and useful finite-time retention explains how structural fragility can coexist with functional robustness. The authors therefore argue that continuous attractors remain a useful analogy for analog memory despite their sensitivity as exact mathematical objects.
neurips-2024-back-to-the-continuous-attr.tldr: Perturbed continuous attractors can retain useful finite-time memory through a surviving slow manifold, despite losing their exact attractor structure.

paragraphs: CriticEval measures how well language models identify and correct flaws in responses. This ability matters when models are used to improve their own outputs or help oversee other systems. The paper addresses a measurement problem: existing evaluations cover too narrow a range of critique behavior or provide insufficiently reliable judgments of critique quality.

The benchmark spans four dimensions of critique across nine task scenarios. It includes numerical assessments and written critiques, and it varies the quality of the responses being evaluated. This design examines whether a model can critique across several conditions. A large collection of annotated critiques supplies references that support GPT-4's evaluation of written feedback.

Evaluations of both open-source and closed-source models support the reliability of the benchmark's assessment procedure. The results also indicate promise for open-source models and benefits from critique datasets. Relationships between performance, task type, response quality, and critique dimension show why critique ability needs to be examined from multiple angles when assessing models for improvement or oversight.
neurips-2024-criticeval-evaluating-large.tldr: CriticEval evaluates language-model critiques across tasks, response qualities, and critique formats using annotated references to support reliable assessment.

paragraphs: Multimodal models often learn from paired inputs and are expected to receive all those input types when used. In practice, privacy constraints or collection difficulties can leave some modalities unavailable. Models trained with complete inputs can then perform poorly. This paper adapts pretrained multimodal models to visual recognition under different patterns of missing information.

The approach uses prompt learning, treating each missing-modality case as a distinct input condition. It designs prompts around relationships between prompts and input features, as well as relationships among prompts at different network layers. It also uses the complementary meaning carried by different modalities to guide the prompts for each one. These connections make prompt design responsive to both the available information and the model's internal representations.

Experiments on three datasets report consistent improvements over previous approaches across the tested missing-modality scenarios. Additional ablations examine different missing proportions and types, supporting the method's reliability and generalizability within those evaluations. The findings suggest that coordinated prompting can help adapt existing multimodal models when their usual input assumptions break down.
neurips-2024-deep-correlated-prompting-f.tldr: Correlated prompts help pretrained multimodal models handle missing inputs by coordinating information across features, layers, and modalities.

paragraphs: FunCoder addresses the difficulty language models face when generating programs with complex requirements. Planning every detail in advance can be difficult, while improving code through self-generated tests depends on those tests being correct. The framework combines dynamic decomposition into functions with a behavior-based way of choosing among implementations.

During generation, FunCoder recursively creates smaller sub-functions, organizing them into a tree of goals. The completed pieces are composed to accomplish larger objectives. It also uses functional consensus: similarities in program behavior help determine which functions to select. This is intended to reduce the propagation of errors from individual pieces into the assembled program.

Across HumanEval, MBPP, xCodeEval, and MATH with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, the authors report an average improvement of 9.8% over state-of-the-art methods. With FunCoder, StableCode-3b also surpasses GPT-3.5 and reaches 97.7% of GPT-4's performance on HumanEval. Further analysis finds that dynamic decomposition handles complex requirements and that functional consensus outperforms self-testing for correctness evaluation in the studied setting.
neurips-2024-divide-and-conquer-meets-co.tldr: FunCoder improves code generation by recursively composing smaller functions and selecting implementations through agreement in program behavior.

paragraphs: Sequential recommendation tries to follow how a user's interests change across interactions. Many methods effectively treat successive interactions as equally spaced, even though real gaps vary considerably. The paper focuses on the associated uncertainty: as more time passes without an interaction, the user's behavior becomes less certain. It aims to make that timing relevant to both predictions and confidence.

The proposed E-NSDE combines a neural stochastic differential equation with evidential learning. The differential equation models a continuously evolving user representation, allowing behavior to change between observed interactions. Evidential learning estimates uncertainty associated with behavior and with the model's knowledge, taking the time gap into account when assigning confidence to a prediction.

The authors also derive a mathematical relationship between elapsed interaction time and model uncertainty, which guides learning. Experiments on real-world data show the method's effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution brings temporal evolution and uncertainty estimation into a single recommendation framework, making the spacing of observations part of how the model reasons about changing interests.
neurips-2024-evidential-stochastic-diffe.tldr: E-NSDE models continuously changing user interests and links prediction uncertainty to the time between interactions.

paragraphs: ExRAP helps embodied agents follow ongoing instructions in environments that change over time. A planner needs information about its surroundings, but previously observed facts can become outdated. Exploring constantly also consumes effort. The framework combines environmental memory, retrieval, and exploration so that language-model planning can respond to the current context.

Each instruction becomes a set of queries to environmental memory and actions conditioned on the answers. Exploration is integrated into planning through an information-based scheme, helping the agent balance obtaining fresh information against the burden of investigating its environment. Memory-assisted query evaluation supports multiple tasks performed continually and simultaneously. A temporal consistency refinement further addresses the decay of stored knowledge.

Experiments in VirtualHome, ALFRED, and CARLA cover different instruction types, task scales, and degrees of environmental change. ExRAP consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art language-model planners in goal success and execution efficiency. These findings support the value of managing the freshness of environmental knowledge as part of planning, especially when several instructions must be carried out in changing surroundings.
neurips-2024-exploratory-retrieval-augme.tldr: ExRAP combines memory retrieval and planned exploration to help embodied agents complete ongoing tasks in changing environments.

paragraphs: GraphVis explores how knowledge graphs can support language-model reasoning while preserving their structure. Existing approaches commonly turn graph relationships into linear sequences of text triples, which the authors argue are less expressive than the original graph. GraphVis instead presents graph structure visually to a large vision-language model.

The model learns through a curriculum with two stages. First, it learns to recognize basic graphical features in images. It then learns to answer questions using visual graphs. This ordering connects graph-image comprehension with reasoning over the represented knowledge. Synthetic graph images also provide additional training material that can benefit visual question answering.

On commonsense question-answering benchmarks, GraphVis reports an average improvement of 11.1% over its base model and outperforms the compared knowledge-graph-enhanced language-model methods. It also improves zero-shot visual question answering, with a reported gain of 4.32% on benchmarks such as ScienceQA that contain related scientific diagrams. Together, these results suggest that learning to interpret visual graph structure can benefit both textual reasoning and some diagram-related visual tasks.
neurips-2024-graphvis-boosting-llms-with.tldr: GraphVis teaches vision-language models to interpret knowledge graphs as images, improving textual and visual question answering in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: HHD-GP learns dynamical systems using a model whose structure reflects physical properties. The paper addresses a concern with physics-agnostic machine learning: a model may recognize patterns without making the underlying system understandable, robustly represented, or efficient to learn from limited data. Its approach builds a physical decomposition directly into a Gaussian process.

The Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition separates the learned dynamics into curl-free and divergence-free components. These describe different structural aspects of a vector field, and the framework learns both simultaneously. Expressing the model this way allows it to incorporate symmetry priors. The authors show that these priors improve prediction and make the model identifiable, allowing learned features to be associated with understandable scientific properties.

On several benchmark dynamical systems, HHD-GP achieves better predictive performance than the compared baselines. It also produces physically meaningful decompositions from noisy and sparse observations. The contribution therefore connects predictive accuracy with interpretability: the same structured representation used to forecast behavior also exposes components that help explain the system being modeled.
neurips-2024-hhd-gp-incorporating-helmho.tldr: HHD-GP builds physical decompositions and symmetry priors into Gaussian processes to learn interpretable dynamics from noisy, sparse data.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can learn undesirable behavior because their goals are misaligned, rewards are scarce, or it is difficult to determine which actions deserve credit. Deep neural networks make these problems harder for domain experts to inspect. This paper introduces Successive Concept Bottleneck Agents, or SCoBots, to make an agent's decision process more accessible to human understanding and revision.

SCoBots use consecutive concept bottleneck layers that represent information through interpretable concepts. Their representation includes both properties of individual objects and relationships between objects. This matters because many reinforcement learning tasks depend on how objects relate to one another. The successive layers provide a structured representation through which experts can examine behavior and guide its regularization.

Experiments provide evidence that SCoBots achieve competitive performance while offering opportunities for expert inspection and intervention. In Pong, the approach exposed a previously unknown misalignment problem and enabled the authors to resolve it. This example supports the practical value of interpretable internal representations for improving alignment, alongside the reported evidence that transparency can coexist with competitive task performance.
neurips-2024-interpretable-concept-bottl.tldr: SCoBots use interpretable object and relationship concepts to help experts inspect and correct reinforcement-learning behavior.

paragraphs: A task vector records how a model's weights change when a pretrained model is fine-tuned for a particular task. Arithmetic on these vectors can combine specialized representations. This paper asks whether different blocks within a task vector should contribute differently when transferring or combining knowledge, and introduces aTLAS to learn those contributions.

aTLAS assigns different learned coefficients to parameter blocks and combines them linearly. This produces anisotropic scaling: different parts of a task vector receive different amounts of emphasis. Only a small number of coefficients need to be learned, exploiting the low intrinsic dimensionality of pretrained models. Reusing already learned blocks also supports modular learning with reduced dependence on large datasets.

Experiments cover task arithmetic, few-shot recognition, and test-time adaptation using supervised or unsupervised objectives. Learned block scaling reduces interference among composed task vectors, while composition performs well with few or no labels and shows greater resilience to domain shift. Selecting informative blocks before training can also reduce memory requirements. The authors further demonstrate potential for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and scaling to higher performance.
neurips-2024-knowledge-composition-using.tldr: aTLAS learns how strongly to combine blocks of task vectors, improving knowledge transfer with relatively few trainable coefficients.

paragraphs: Medical time series contain variables that are measured at irregular intervals, evolve differently, and remain connected to one another. Capturing those individual patterns and cross-variable relationships together is difficult. KEDGN addresses this by using textual medical knowledge to shape a dynamic graph model of the measurements.

A pretrained language model converts descriptions of each variable's medical properties into semantic representations. These representations guide the allocation of variable-specific parameter spaces for learning temporal patterns and the construction of a graph describing medical relationships among variables. A density-aware mechanism adjusts the graph at different timestamps, allowing its relationships to vary as the sequence develops.

The variable-specific parameters and changing graph are incorporated into a graph convolutional recurrent network. This combines learning about each variable's history with learning about dependencies between variables. Across four healthcare datasets, the authors report significant improvements over existing methods. The results support using medical descriptions to organize time-series modeling, so that variable identity and changing relationships both inform how irregular observations are interpreted.
neurips-2024-knowledge-empowered-dynamic.tldr: KEDGN uses textual medical knowledge and dynamic graphs to model individual variables and their changing relationships in irregular medical time series.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a single neuron when labels can be arbitrary and the data distribution can shift adversarially. The goal is to find a best-fitting predictor under squared error while accounting for unfavorable distributions near a reference distribution. Closeness is measured using chi-squared divergence, and the formal objective penalizes distribution changes according to that divergence.

The authors develop a computationally efficient primal-dual algorithm that addresses the predictor and adversarial distribution within one optimization framework. Its analysis directly controls the original nonconvex squared loss. The target predictor has bounded weight norm, and the guarantee is expressed using a predictor-distribution pair attaining the stated minimax objective.

Under that witness distribution, the learned neuron's error is at most a dimension-independent constant greater than one times the target neuron's error, plus an additive tolerance. This is an approximation guarantee relative to the best-fit objective, so it accommodates irreducible error from arbitrary labels. The work also identifies a route for analyzing primal-dual optimization when the nonconvexity has exploitable structure.
neurips-2024-learning-a-single-neuron-ro.tldr: A primal-dual algorithm learns a single neuron with a constant-factor squared-error guarantee under a chi-squared-penalized adversarial distribution objective.

paragraphs: Manifold Free-Form Flows, or M-FFF, model probability distributions on spaces with geometric constraints. Existing approaches that work on arbitrary manifolds can be expensive when generating samples because they must solve a differential equation. This paper develops a method that generates a sample with a single function evaluation, targeting that inference cost directly.

The approach adapts the free-form flow framework to Riemannian manifolds, enabling a neural network to be trained through maximum likelihood on the manifold itself. Its stated applicability depends on having a known projection onto the manifold. That condition provides a way to adapt the framework across different geometries while retaining a common modeling approach.

In the reported comparisons, M-FFF consistently matches or exceeds previous single-step methods designed for particular manifolds. It is typically about two orders of magnitude faster than multi-step diffusion or flow-matching methods and achieves better likelihoods in several experiments. These findings support the possibility of combining broadly adaptable geometric modeling with inexpensive sampling, without making the reported speed or likelihood advantage a universal guarantee.
neurips-2024-learning-distributions-on-m.tldr: M-FFF learns manifold-valued distributions through maximum likelihood and generates samples in a single function evaluation.

paragraphs: Muscles in Time, or MinT, addresses the scarcity of muscle activation data for studying human movement. Observing poses reveals how the body moves, while muscle activity provides another level of information about the muscular and skeletal processes involved. Collecting ground-truth activations is resource-intensive, so the authors create a large synthetic dataset through biomechanical simulation.

The pipeline starts with existing motion-capture sequences and enriches them using human body models in OpenSim. From pose sequences, it produces simulated information about when muscles activate during movement. MinT contains more than nine hours of simulation data across 227 subjects and 402 simulated muscle strands, linking motion observations with detailed activation sequences.

The authors demonstrate the dataset's utility by training two different sequence-to-sequence neural network architectures to estimate muscle activations from human poses. These results establish a use for MinT in learning the relationship between visible movement and simulated muscular activity. The synthetic nature of the activations is central to the contribution: biomechanical modeling supplies the additional information used to enrich existing motion data.
neurips-2024-muscles-in-time-learning-to.tldr: MinT enriches motion-capture data with simulated muscle activations and supports learning to estimate those activations from pose sequences.

paragraphs: LATEC examines how to compare explainable AI methods when evaluation choices can change the apparent winner. Existing studies often consider few methods or metrics and overlook factors such as model architecture and input modality. This makes it difficult for practitioners to distinguish a dependable recommendation from a ranking shaped by a narrow experimental setup.

The benchmark evaluates 17 explanation methods using 20 metrics across varied architectures and input modalities, covering 7,560 combinations. This broad design reveals substantial disagreement among metrics and a resulting risk of unreliable rankings. The authors propose a more robust evaluation scheme and compare methods with the aim of helping practitioners choose according to their needs.

Expected Gradients emerges as the top-performing method in this evaluation, despite being absent from the relevant related studies considered by the authors. LATEC also releases 326,000 saliency maps and 378,000 metric scores for further evaluation research. The findings make evaluation design part of the explanation-selection problem: confidence in a ranking depends on understanding how its metrics and experimental settings shape it.
neurips-2024-navigating-the-maze-of-expl.tldr: LATEC shows how conflicting explanation metrics can produce unreliable rankings and provides a broader benchmark and more robust evaluation scheme.

paragraphs: First-order optimization usually advances through a chain of updates, with each iteration depending on the preceding one. That sequential dependency can make convergence slow even when parallel computing resources are available. OptEx aims to reduce the number of sequential iterations by approximately parallelizing parts of this update process.

The framework predicts gradients needed by upcoming iterations using a kernelized estimator trained on previously evaluated gradients. These predictions help loosen the dependency between successive updates. The authors establish bounds on gradient estimation error and analyze the iteration complexity of an SGD-based version. Their theory shows estimation error tending to zero as the gradient history accumulates.

For the analyzed SGD-based method, parallelism of N yields an effective acceleration rate proportional to the square root of N in the sequential iterations required for convergence. This statement concerns iteration complexity, rather than a blanket wall-clock speedup. Empirical studies on synthetic functions, reinforcement learning, and neural network training also report substantial practical efficiency improvements, supporting gradient prediction as a way to exploit parallel resources across optimization steps.
neurips-2024-optex-expediting-first-orde.tldr: OptEx predicts upcoming gradients from optimization history to approximately parallelize iterations and reduce sequential optimization work.

paragraphs: PACE targets electromagnetic field simulation for complex photonic devices, where numerical computation can slow design and validation. Learning-based alternatives struggle with scattering, resonance, sensitivity to local geometry, and rich frequency information. These challenges require a model to connect detailed device structures with field behavior across the entire simulation domain.

The proposed cross-axis factorized operator is designed to capture those long-distance relationships. For especially difficult cases, PACE also uses a two-stage process: one model predicts an initial solution and a second refines it. This divides a challenging simulation into an initial estimation problem followed by a correction problem, improving fidelity for more intricate devices.

Across the reported device benchmarks, a single PACE model achieves 73% lower error with 50% fewer parameters than the compared recent machine-learning PDE solvers. The two-stage setup improves fidelity further for harder cases. Reported runtime advantages range from 154–577 times over a SciPy numerical solver and 11.8–12 times over a highly optimized Pardiso solver, illustrating that the speed advantage depends on the numerical comparison.
neurips-2024-pace-pacing-operator-learni.tldr: PACE combines long-range operator learning with optional two-stage refinement to improve the accuracy and speed of complex photonic field simulation.

paragraphs: Neuroscientists sometimes train recurrent neural networks to reproduce recorded neural activity and then analyze those networks to infer how a biological circuit works. This paper examines the reliability of that procedure when recordings cover only part of a circuit. Even large recordings can represent a small fraction of the neurons in the system of interest.

The authors study simulated teacher networks and student networks fitted to their observed activity. They show that partial observation can produce a student with different underlying mechanisms even when individual-unit dynamics match. In particular, partially observed systems with functionally feedforward or low-rank connectivity can yield fitted models containing spurious attractor structure.

An attractor inferred from the student can therefore suggest a dynamical explanation that does not faithfully describe the teacher. The result establishes that agreement with observed activity can coexist with mechanistic mismatch in these settings. It highlights the challenge of recovering neural mechanisms from single-trial data and motivates additional ways of validating data-constrained dynamical models before using their internal structure to explain neural computation.
neurips-2024-partial-observation-can-ind.tldr: Fitting partially observed neural activity can produce recurrent models with spurious attractors despite matching individual-unit dynamics.

paragraphs: SpikedAttention converts trained transformers into networks that operate end to end using spikes. Spiking neural networks offer a route toward lower energy consumption, but transformer self-attention is difficult to express through spike-based computation. Previous transformer-based spiking approaches have therefore changed the attention architecture or retained computations that do not use spikes.

The proposed conversion preserves the trained transformer's attention architecture and requires neither conversion-aware training nor post-training. Its spike-based handling of attention makes it possible to apply the conversion to both a vision transformer and BERT. Preserving the architecture is central to the contribution because it allows the method to work directly with already trained transformers.

The converted Swin model achieves 80.0% ImageNet accuracy with 28.7 million parameters. Its reported energy consumption is 42% lower than Swin-T when accounting for weight accumulation, neuron-potential updates, and on-chip data movement. For BERT on GLUE, the authors report an average accuracy loss of only 0.3% and 58% lower energy consumption. These results demonstrate favorable accuracy and energy tradeoffs for the evaluated conversions.
neurips-2024-spikedattention-training-fr.tldr: SpikedAttention converts trained transformers into fully spike-driven networks without additional training or changes to their attention architecture.

paragraphs: TrackIME improves video point tracking by narrowing where a model searches for a point across frames. Searching broadly is computationally demanding, while reducing frame resolution discards details needed for precise trajectories. The method uses object-level motion to focus computation on relevant image regions while preserving their resolution.

It estimates an object's trajectory by tracking a group of points belonging to that object and aggregating their movements. Regions that do not contain the object can then be removed from the search. The framework also combines tracking with segmentation to handle occlusion. Object masks help the tracker avoid occluded points, and improved tracks can in turn produce better segmentation masks.

This interaction lets the two tasks support one another while the object trajectory constrains the tracking search. The framework can be incorporated into various tracking models. On TAP-Vid, it improves all evaluated baselines, with gains of up to 13.5% on the average Jaccard metric. The reported results support using object-level structure to preserve tracking detail without relying on broad, full-frame correspondence searches.
neurips-2024-trackime-enhanced-video-poi.tldr: TrackIME uses object motion and segmentation to narrow point-tracking searches while retaining image detail and handling occlusion.

paragraphs: This paper studies sparse linear regression when the data come from self-interested people who care about privacy. The setting combines a statistical goal, estimating the underlying parameters accurately, with an incentive problem: participants may prefer to misreport their information. The authors seek a mechanism that protects reports while making truthful participation attractive to most agents.

They derive a private estimator with a closed-form expression and build a computation and payment scheme around it. With an appropriate design, the mechanism satisfies joint differential privacy and makes truthful reporting an approximate Bayes Nash equilibrium for a fraction of agents approaching one. The equilibrium qualification means the incentive guarantee allows a small potential benefit from deviating.

The stated asymptotic results also allow estimation error to approach zero as the number of agents increases. Individual rationality holds for a fraction of participants approaching one, while the analyst's required payment budget tends to zero. These guarantees connect statistical accuracy, privacy, and incentives within one mechanism. Their scope is explicitly approximate and applies to nearly all agents, with the favorable quantities expressed through large-sample rates.
neurips-2024-truthful-high-dimensional-s.tldr: A private regression estimator and payment mechanism jointly support accurate estimation and approximately truthful participation by nearly all agents.

paragraphs: UniFL addresses three goals in text-to-image diffusion: better visual quality, stronger aesthetic appeal, and faster generation. The paper treats these as connected targets for feedback-based learning. Its framework is intended to improve different latent diffusion models, with SD1.5 and SDXL given as examples of its applicability.

The framework contains three components with distinct roles. Perceptual feedback learning targets visual quality, decoupled feedback learning targets aesthetics, and adversarial feedback learning targets inference acceleration. Bringing them into one framework allows generation quality and computational efficiency to be pursued together. The design therefore covers both how an image looks and how quickly the model can produce it.

Experiments and user studies support improvements in image quality and accelerated inference. The authors report a 17% user-preference advantage over ImageReward for generation quality. At four inference steps, they report general-preference advantages of 57% over LCM and 20% over SDXL Turbo. These are preference results under the reported comparisons, showing that the accelerated generation setup can also produce outputs users favor.
neurips-2024-unifl-improve-latent-diffus.tldr: UniFL combines perceptual, aesthetic, and adversarial feedback to improve diffusion image quality while accelerating generation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way for learned dynamical models to adapt at runtime without gradient calculations or retraining. Autonomous systems may encounter conditions outside their training examples, making rapid identification of their current dynamics useful. The approach draws on function encoders, combining neural-network flexibility with the structure of Hilbert spaces.

During training, it learns a collection of neural ordinary differential equation basis functions. Together, these functions span a space of dynamics. After training, an efficient inner-product calculation identifies dynamics within that learned space. The runtime adaptation is therefore a calculation over the learned representation, with its stated scope tied to the dynamics that representation can express.

The authors report state-of-the-art system-modeling accuracy in two MuJoCo robot environments. They also show that the learned models support more efficient model predictive control of a quadrotor. These results connect the representation method to both prediction and control, demonstrating how a learned family of dynamical systems can enable rapid transfer without an online optimization phase based on gradients.
neurips-2024-zero-shot-transfer-of-neura.tldr: A learned basis of neural ODEs enables runtime identification of dynamics through inner products, without gradients or retraining.
